patches.old: This principle is why camouflage works: when an animal's outline is interrupted by patterns that align with background contours, the figure-ground boundary is disrupted and the animal becomes harder to detect.
patches.new: Good continuation is one of the principles camouflage exploits, though not the main one. The primary mechanism of camouflage is **similarity**: matching the colour, texture and pattern of the background means the hidden figure shares features with the ground, so figure-ground segregation never gets started. Good continuation is exploited in addition by *disruptive* patterning — bold shapes that run across an animal's outline and join up with background contours, so the eye follows a smooth path straight past the real edge of the body. Expect a question about plain camouflage to be keyed to similarity, and one about outline-breaking stripes or blotches to involve good continuation.

patches.old: Common fate is tempting but refers to elements moving together being grouped, which is not the primary mechanism of static camouflage.
patches.new: Common fate is tempting but refers to elements moving together being grouped, which is not the primary mechanism of static camouflage. Continuity is the next best distractor: disruptive patterns that run across an outline do exploit good continuation, but that is a secondary effect, whereas matching colour and texture to the background — similarity — is what the stem actually describes.

visual.caption: Lose an eye and only the bottom two cues go. That is why monocular observers judge distance well while moving and poorly while sitting still.
